items.prompt: Two `setTimeout(..., 0)` callbacks are due in the same tick; the first one (B) queues a promise handler (C), the second logs D. Why is the output B, C, D rather than B, D, C?
items.answer: Microtasks drain after each macrotask callback, so C runs between the two timers
distractors: Same-tick timers merge into one callback, and promise handlers run inside it in order
The timers phase pauses whenever a promise is created and resumes once it settles
C was registered before D in the source, and each queue is ordered by source position
items.explanation: Microtasks are drained after each macrotask callback, not after the whole phase: two timers due together are still two callbacks with a full checkpoint between them.

items.prompt: `async function buildReport() { const rows = crunch(200000); await save(rows); }` is called from a request handler, and the server freezes while it runs. A teammate says "it's async, it can't block". What is wrong with that claim?
items.answer: Code before the first await runs synchronously, so crunch() blocks the caller
distractors: async moves the body onto a worker thread, so the freeze comes from save() instead
Async calls are queued as macrotasks, so crunch() waits behind pending timers
The body is deferred to the microtask queue, so a microtask backlog is to blame
items.explanation: Everything before the first await runs synchronously at the call site, so crunch() occupies the stack; only the continuation after await is deferred. await desugars to 'return a promise now and register the rest as a .then handler'; an async function doing expensive work before its first await blocks the caller completely.

items.prompt: The same eight lines print nextTick callbacks before promise callbacks as `.cjs` but after them as `.mjs`. What explains the flip, and which ordering rule should you rely on?
items.answer: ESM top level runs inside a promise job; rely on in-callback order, same in both
distractors: ESM disables process.nextTick until the graph loads; rely on queueMicrotask first
Node runs .mjs in a separate event loop; rely on nextTick beating promise callbacks
The .mjs loader sorts callbacks by queue name; rely on promises beating nextTick
items.explanation: An ES module's top level is evaluated inside a promise job, so the microtask drain is already running and top-level microtasks keep draining before the loop returns to the nextTick checkpoint. Inside a callback: nextTick drains, then microtasks, in both module systems.

items.prompt: At the top level of a CommonJS file, `setTimeout(f, 0)` vs `setImmediate(g)` order varies run to run. Inside an `fs.readFile` callback, g always runs before f. Why?
items.answer: The callback runs in the poll phase, and check is the very next phase after it
distractors: Inside I/O callbacks Node clamps setTimeout to 4 ms, so the immediate finishes first
readFile callbacks run on the libuv thread pool, where setImmediate runs synchronously
setImmediate is a microtask and setTimeout a macrotask, so the immediate wins there
items.explanation: You are already in the poll phase, so check is next; timers only come round on the next loop iteration. 'Run right after the current I/O, before any timers' is why setImmediate exists. At top level the 1 ms clamp races process startup.

items.prompt: A long CPU loop is chunked, with `await Promise.resolve()` between chunks so that timers and incoming requests get a turn. They still starve. Why, and what should the yield be?
items.answer: The microtask queue drains before the loop moves on; yield via setImmediate instead
distractors: Promise.resolve() is cached, so later awaits resolve synchronously; await a fresh value
The chunks are too large; the same await yields fine once each chunk is under 1 ms
await yields to the loop just inside I/O callbacks; wrap the loop in fs.readFile
items.explanation: Both prioritised queues drain to empty, so yielding to the microtask queue never lets timers or I/O run. `await new Promise(r => setImmediate(r))` yields to the check phase, a macrotask.

items.prompt: After swapping native promises for a userland promise library in one module, two async chains that used to interleave now interleave one step differently, though both still finish correctly. What is the most likely mechanism?
items.answer: Awaiting a non-native thenable costs one extra microtask, so it resumes a tick later
distractors: Userland promises run their handlers as macrotasks, so they wait behind pending timers
The library resolves synchronously, so the awaiting function stops yielding to the loop
V8 skips the second await of a non-native promise, so one chain step is dropped
items.explanation: The engine must wrap a thenable. Native promises get a fast path (1 tick); a thenable costs one tick more. If two chains interleave 'wrongly', count ticks before assuming a bug.

items.prompt: A handler calls `sendAnalytics()` (an async function) without awaiting it, planning to attach `.catch(log)` inside a `setTimeout(..., 50)`. On Node 22 the call rejects. What happens?
items.answer: The process crashes: rejections are checked at the checkpoint, before the timer
distractors: The error is logged normally: Node waits until the timer attaches the catch
The rejection is silently dropped, because no caller awaited the promise
A deprecation warning is printed: the process stays alive until the next GC
items.explanation: Since Node 15 the default is --unhandled-rejections=throw, checked at the end of the microtask checkpoint; attaching .catch later in the same tick is fine, in a setTimeout it is far too late. Fire and forget is fire and crash.

items.prompt: `setTimeout(log2, 0); Promise.resolve().then(() => setTimeout(log3, 0)); setTimeout(() => Promise.resolve().then(log4), 0);` prints 2 4 3. Why does 3 come last even though its .then ran before any timer?
items.answer: The .then only queues a new timer, which lines up behind the two earlier timers
distractors: Timers created inside microtasks are clamped to 4 ms, so log3's timer is due later
The timers queue runs in reverse registration order whenever promises are involved
A timer queued from a .then runs in the check phase, after the timers phase ends
items.explanation: The .then schedules a new timer, which joins the timers queue behind the two registered synchronously; a promise handler gives no priority to the work it queues. Timers fire in the order they became due; track what each callback queues, not just when it runs.

items.prompt: A Node service stops responding and no timers fire. Which observation points at microtask/nextTick starvation rather than a deadlock?
items.answer: The CPU is pegged at 100% while hung, whereas a deadlock leaves it idle
distractors: The heap grows steadily until the process is eventually OOM-killed
A debugger shows two stack frames waiting on each other's lock
The process exits with code 0 right after the last timer is cleared
items.explanation: Recursive nextTick, recursive Promise.then and a sync loop all look identical from outside: CPU pegged, responsive to nothing, timers never fire.

items.prompt: `button.addEventListener('click', cart.checkout)` throws "Cannot read properties of undefined" inside checkout (an ESM module), while `cart.checkout()` works. Why?
items.answer: this is set at the call site; called without a dot, it falls back to undefined
distractors: Passing a method as an argument copies it, and the copy loses the cart's fields
Event listeners set this to the window object, which lacks the cart's own fields
checkout was defined in another module, so this refers to that module's scope
items.explanation: this is part of the call, not the function. The listener calls the bare function with no dot, so implicit binding (rule 3, receiver) cannot apply and strict default binding (rule 4) gives undefined in ESM. Fix with bind or an arrow wrapper.

items.prompt: `function P(x, y) { this.x = x; this.y = y; }` and `const P1 = P.bind({ ignored: true }, 1)`. What does `new P1(2)` produce, and why?
items.answer: A fresh {x: 1, y: 2}: new drops the bound receiver but keeps the bound argument
distractors: The { ignored: true } object, now holding x and y, since bind outranks new
A TypeError: a bound function is not constructible with new
A fresh {x: 2, y: undefined}: new discards the receiver and bound argument
items.explanation: new is the highest-priority rule: it builds a new object as this even after bind, discarding the bound receiver while keeping bound arguments.

items.prompt: In an ESM file, `const counter = { n: 0, inc: () => this.n++ }` and `counter.inc()` throws. A callback `items.forEach(i => this.total += i)` inside a regular method works fine. What distinguishes the two?
items.answer: Arrows take this lexically: the callback gets the method's, inc gets module scope
distractors: Arrows bind this to the object literal: forEach invokes the callback through it
Object literals freeze arrow-valued properties: this.n++ fails, shorthand works
counter.inc() passes counter as this, but arrows reject plain-object receivers
items.explanation: Arrows have no this of their own. The method's callback inherits the method's this, but an arrow used as the object method itself has no enclosing method, so this is module scope (undefined in ESM). Arrows for callbacks, methods for methods.

items.prompt: A base class has `static create(n) { return new Animal(n); }` and `class Dog extends Animal`. `Dog.create('Rex')` returns an object without Dog's methods. What change fixes it, and why does it work?
items.answer: Use new this(n), since in a static method this is the class it was called on
distractors: Redeclare create in each subclass, since statics are not inherited via extends
Use new super(n), since super in a static method is the calling subclass
Use Object.create(Animal.prototype), since new in a static skips subclass constructors
items.explanation: Inside a static method this is the class it was called on, so Dog.create builds a Dog. extends wires the class-to-class chain too (Object.getPrototypeOf(Dog) === Animal), so statics are inherited; hard-coding new Animal silently breaks every subclass.

items.front: A word counter does `counts[word] = (counts[word] || 0) + 1` with `const counts = {}` over user-submitted text. One document contains the word "toString". What does its count become?
items.back: 'function toString() { [native code] }1': the plain object inherits toString from Object.prototype, so the lookup is not undefined and + concatenates. No error, just a corrupt value downstream. Fix: Object.create(null), a Map, or Object.hasOwn checks.

items.front: A base class constructor calls `this.render()`; a subclass overrides render() and reads its own field `label = 'Save'`. On construction the button renders "undefined". Why?
items.back: Init order is base field, base constructor body, derived field, derived constructor body: the override runs before the subclass's fields are assigned. Fix: do not call overridable methods from a constructor, or pass the values as arguments.

items.front: An API endpoint accepts 5 MB JSON uploads and calls `JSON.parse` on them in the handler. Dashboards show p50 latency fine but p99 terrible across ALL endpoints. What is going on?
items.back: Each ~300 ms synchronous parse blocks the event loop, delaying every concurrent request, not just the upload. Fix: keep large CPU work off the JS thread (worker, streaming parser) or chunk and yield; watch it with monitorEventLoopDelay.

items.front: Legacy code sets `Dog.prototype = { bark() {} }` and a serializer later uses `obj.constructor.name` to tag records. Dog records are tagged "Object". Why?
items.back: constructor is an ordinary writable property on the prototype; replacing the prototype wholesale discards it, so lookup falls through to Object.prototype.constructor. Fix: add methods to the existing prototype (or use class), or restore constructor explicitly.
